title: Spotting bias in a source
log: 2026-11-04T18:10:11Z recheck: the fresh check agreed with the fix, cleared with the fix

draft.title: Spotting bias in a source
card: A source is biased when it leans one way. This can happen because of who made it, who paid for it, or what the maker wants the reader to do.
Ask who made the source and why. A group that gains from a result may show only the facts that support it.
Compare the source with other sources, ideally from makers with different interests. If they disagree, find out why.
Look for data, such as figures with a clear period and method. Opinion and emotive words give less evidence than data. A biased source can still contain true facts, so check them.
draft.remember: Ask who made it and why, then compare it with other sources and check the data.

a.q: A report says a new mine will bring great wealth to a town. It was paid for by the mining company. What is the best reason to check it against other sources?
opts: The company gains if readers support the mine
The report is false because a company paid for it
Company reports never include any data
A report about a mine cannot be about wealth
a.why: The company gains from a positive view, so the report may show only the facts that help it. That does not make every fact false, so the sensible step is to compare it with other sources.
a.clue: Think about who gains if readers agree.

b.q: Two reports on a proposed wind farm in Tasmania disagree. One is from a group of nearby landholders who oppose it. The other is from a wind energy company. What is the best way to judge them?
opts: Compare both with a third source and check their data
Trust the landholders, because they live nearby
Trust the company, because it uses more figures
Ignore both, because every source is biased
b.why: Both makers have an interest, so each may lean one way. Comparing them with a third source and checking the data is the sound step. Dropping both, or trusting one for living nearby, skips that check.
b.clue: Both makers have something to gain.

a.best: The company gains if readers support the mine

b.best: Compare both with a third source and check their data

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about who gains if readers agree' repeats the words 'gains' and 'readers'. Only the right option uses those words, so a student can match the wording without knowing the idea.
The distractor 'Company reports never include any data' uses 'never'. That absolute marks it as wrong without testing the idea, and the card says only that a group 'may' show selected facts.

check.summary: The card and both answers are correct. In question a, the clue echoes the right option's wording and one distractor uses 'never', so a student could pick the answer without understanding bias.
